inline.s: Ananda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how long was the lifespan of that Tathagata, the King of Sovereignty over the World?”

The World-Honored One told him: “The lifespan of that Buddha was fully forty kalpas. Ananda, the Buddha-lands of those twenty-one koṭis of Buddhas, the Buddha-land embraced by the monk Dharmakara, surpasses them. Having embraced them all, he went to where the Tathagata King of Sovereignty over the World was. He bowed his head at his feet, circled him seven times to the right, and stood to one side, saying: ‘Lord, I have embraced and gathered in a Buddha-land perfect in merit, virtue, and adornment.’
The Buddha said: “Now is the very time. You should tell it fully, so that the assembly may rejoice, and so that the great assembly may all embrace that Buddha-land and bring it to perfection.”
Dharmakara said: “May the World-Honored One in his great compassion stay and listen; I shall now set forth my peerless vows:
If I attain supreme bodhi, and there be in my land beings of the hells, of the hungry ghosts, or of the animal realm, may I never take supreme, perfect enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and there be beings in my land who fall into the three evil destinies, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land are not all of one true golden hue, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land differ in form and feature, some fair and some foul, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land do not gain the memory of past lives, down to not knowing the affairs of a hundred thousand kalpas in koṭis of nayutas, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land, lacking the celestial eye, cannot see even the Buddha-lands of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land do not obtain the celestial ear, and cannot hear the Buddha teaching the Dharma even beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of yojanas, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land have no knowledge of the minds of others, and do not know the mental conduct of the beings in the Buddha-lands of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land do not obtain spiritual powers, mastery, and the perfections, so that in a single instant of thought they cannot pass beyond the Buddha-lands of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and beings in my land give rise to even the least thought of “I” and “mine,” may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and beings in my land are not certain to accomplish equal, perfect enlightenment and realize the great nirvana, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and my light is limited, so that it does not illumine even the Buddha-lands of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas and beyond reckoning, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and my lifespan is limited, even to koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas and beyond reckoning, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and there be any in my land who know the number of its hearers: even were the three-thousand-great-thousand world filled with beings and with pratyekabuddhas who for a hundred thousand years exhausted their wisdom to reckon it, they could not know it. If there be any who know it, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land have lifespans that are limited and bounded, may I never take bodhi — save for those who are born there by the power of their vows.
If I become a Buddha, and there be in my land any beings with an evil name, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the countless Buddhas in those immeasurable lands do not together proclaim and praise my land, may I never take enlightenment.

If, when I attain supreme enlightenment, beings in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, turn all their roots of goodness, heart to heart, toward rebirth in my land, even to ten thoughts, and are not born there, may I never take bodhi — save for those who commit the five heinous deeds, who slander the true Dharma, and who revile the sages.

If I become a Buddha, and there be beings in other Buddha-lands who arouse the bodhi-mind and give rise to pure thoughts toward me, and who then turn their roots of goodness toward rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and at the end of their lives I and the assembly of monks do not appear before them, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and there be beings in immeasurable lands who hear my name spoken and turn their own roots of goodness toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and are not born there, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in my land do not all perfect the thirty-two marks, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and all the bodhisattvas in that land do not all stand, with respect to the great bodhi, at the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood — save for those great-vowed bodhisattvas who, for the sake of beings, don the armor of diligence, diligently practice for their benefit, cultivate the great nirvana, travel through all Buddha-lands, practice the bodhisattva path, make offerings to all Tathagatas, establish beings as countless as the sands of the Ganges in supreme enlightenment, and whose practiced conduct surpasses what went before, who walk the path of Samantabhadra and thereby gain deliverance — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in my land do not each morning make offerings to the Buddhas of other regions, even to immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and by the Buddha’s majesty return to their own land before the meal — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in that land, whatever offerings they need for the places of the Buddhas, do not plant roots of goodness of every kind, and such things are not brought to perfection, may I never take bodhi.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who expound the essentials of the Dharma do not skillfully enter into and accord with the wisdom of the All-Knowing, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas born in that land do not possess the firm strength of Narayana, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and throughout my land, among all its adornments, there is no being able to expound them fully — even one with the celestial eye cannot know all its varied kinds, forms and colors, and appearances of light — and if any can know and fully expound them, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and my land possesses immeasurable trees of color a hundred thousand yojanas tall, and among the bodhisattvas there are those of inferior roots of goodness who cannot know them, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land who read and recite the scriptures, teach, and expound them do not obtain supreme eloquence, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in my land do not perfect boundless eloquence, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the light and purity of my land is everywhere without equal, illumining immeasurable, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds, showing therein the faces of beings as in a bright mirror — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and within the bounds of my land, on the earth and in the sky, there are not immeasurable kinds of fragrance, and hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of jeweled censers whose fragrance perfumes everywhere throughout the realm of space, that fragrance surpassing the treasures of gods and humans and offered to the Tathagata and the assembly of bodhisattvas — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and throughout the ten directions all the beings of immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled realms who are touched by the Buddha’s majestic light do not attain peace and joy of body and mind surpassing gods and humans — if it is not so, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in the Buddha-lands of immeasurable, inconceivable, unequaled realms, having heard my name, do not realize the dharma of non-arising and obtain dharanis, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and throughout the countless, inconceivable, unequaled Buddha-lands all the women, having heard my name, gain pure faith, arouse the bodhi-mind, and grow weary of the female body, yet in a future life do not forsake the female body, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the assemblies of bodhisattvas in immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled Buddha-lands, having heard my name, gain the dharma of non-arising, and do not cultivate the peerless pure practice until they reach the great bodhi, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and throughout the ten directions, in the Buddha-lands beyond all measure, all the bodhisattvas, having heard my name, do not bow with all five limbs to the ground and cultivate the bodhisattva path with pure hearts, and if the gods and humans do not revere them, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the clothing the beings in my land need does not come at a thought, as when the Buddha says “Come, monk,” and the Dharma robe is naturally upon the body — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and all kinds of beings, as soon as they are born in my land, do not all obtain every requisite, with pure minds and peace and joy like monks who have destroyed the defilements, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the multitudes in my land cannot, as their hearts wish, see the pure lands of the Buddhas and their peerless adornments all appearing among the jewel trees, like faces seen in a bright mirror — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and beings in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, attain bodhi with any of their faculties deficient or their virtues and powers narrow, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, do not all skillfully distinguish the names and words of the supreme samadhis — and while abiding in those samadhis, in a single instant, in the time of a word, cannot make offerings to immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled Buddhas, and do not realize the six samadhis — may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, are not born after the end of their lives into noble and wealthy families, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, do not in due season cultivate the bodhisattva path, gaining pure joy and the abiding of equality, perfect in all roots of goodness, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and bodhisattvas in other regions, having heard my name, all obtain the gate of the samadhi of equality, and abiding in that concentration ever make offerings to immeasurable, unequaled Buddhas, and until bodhi never turn back — if it is not so, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in my land do not naturally hear the Dharma they wish to hear, according to their vows and aspirations — if it is not so, may I never take enlightenment.
If I attain supreme bodhi, and bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, turn back from supreme, perfect enlightenment, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, hearing my name, do not in that very season obtain the first, second, and third patient acceptances, and cannot realize non-retrogression with respect to all Buddhadharmas, may I never take bodhi.
At that time the Buddha told Ananda: “That monk Dharmakara, having made these vows before the Tathagata King of Sovereignty over the World, by the Buddha’s majestic spirit spoke these verses:
Before the Tathagata I make this vow: on the day I attain supreme bodhi.
if these supreme vows are not fulfilled, may I never take the unequaled honored one of the ten powers.
If my heart cannot bear to give without cease, relieving the poor and freeing them from every pain.
benefiting the world and bringing it peace, may I never become the Dharma King who saves the world.
When I attain bodhi and sit in the place of enlightenment, if my fame does not reach throughout the ten directions.
and the immeasurable, boundless Buddha-lands beyond number do not receive it, may I never take the honored one of the ten powers in the world.
Setting out for the unsurpassed great bodhi, if I leave home to seek the realm of desire.
and in that vow have neither mindfulness nor wisdom, may I never become the tamer, the teacher of gods and humans.
May I attain the Tathagata’s immeasurable light, illumining all Buddha-lands in the ten directions.
able to quench all greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cut off the evil destinies of the world.
May I gain the light that opens the pure eye of wisdom, dispelling the darkness of all states of being.
Ending every calamity, leaving none behind, and setting gods and humans in a mighty one’s peace.
Having cultivated my original practice to purity, I shall gain immeasurable, peerless radiance.
outshining the light of sun and moon, of all the gods, and of the maṇi jewels.
The peerless husband, his practice done, becomes a hidden treasure for the poor.
perfect in wholesome dharmas and without equal, he roars the lion’s roar amid the assembly.
In former times I made offerings to the self-awakened ones, and for many kalpas diligently practiced austerities.
seeking the supreme accumulations of wisdom, fulfilling my original vows as the honored one of gods and humans.
The Tathagata’s knowledge and vision is without obstruction, and can comprehend all that is conditioned.
May I become the unequaled one, the supreme wise one, the true guide.
If I am to attain the great bodhi, may these vast vows be truly fulfilled.
and may the three-thousand-great-thousand world be shaken, with gods raining flowers from the sky.
Then let the whole earth tremble, with celestial flowers and music filling the sky.
and a rain of fine sandalwood powder, and a voice proclaiming that in the future he shall become a Buddha.

The Buddha told Ananda: “That monk Dharmakara, before the Tathagata King of Sovereignty over the World and before the gods and humans, the demons and Brahmas, the ascetics and brahmins, and all the rest, broadly made these great and vast vows. They have all been accomplished — a rarity in the world. Having made these vows, he truly abided in them, and in every kind of merit and virtue he was complete in adornment, of vast majesty and purity of Buddha-land. While he cultivated the bodhisattva path in this way, throughout immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he never once gave rise to greed, anger, or delusion, or to thoughts of desire to harm or to hate; nor did he give rise to thoughts of form, sound, scent, taste, or touch. Toward all beings he ever took joy in love and respect, as toward his own kin. His nature was gentle and mild, and he was easy to live with. To those who came seeking he never went against their wishes; with kind words he persuaded and instructed them, and none failed to follow his heart. He nourished himself with whatever he obtained for the support of the body. Desiring little and content, he ever delighted in emptiness and leisure. He was intelligent by nature and clear in understanding, yet without pretense. His nature was tame and compliant, without violence or evil. Toward all beings he ever held compassion and patience. His mind was without deceit or flattery, and without indolence. With kind words he urged himself onward, seeking all pure dharmas. For all beings everywhere he was brave and never turned back. Benefiting the world, his great vows were fulfilled. He served his teachers and honored the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. In the bodhisattva path he ever wore the armor. His heart delighted in stillness and quiet, and he was free of all defilement and attachment. So that beings might ever cultivate pure dharmas, he became foremost among them in the wholesome dharmas. He dwelt in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, in non-action and non-arising, in neither arising nor ceasing, and was without pride or arrogance. And that true one, in walking the bodhisattva path, ever guarded his speech, and never by his speech harmed others or himself. Ever by his speech-karma he benefited himself and others. When he entered royal cities and villages, though he saw many forms, his mind was undefiled. With a pure mind he neither craved nor hated. At that time the bodhisattva himself practiced giving, and also caused others to practice giving. In the perfection of morality and on through the perfection of wisdom, he set the first two practices in motion, and all were brought to perfection. Because he perfected such roots of goodness, wherever he was born, immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of treasuries of jewels welled up of themselves. And he caused immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled and boundless kinds of beings to abide in supreme, perfect enlightenment. Thus immeasurable bodhisattvas set in motion wondrous practices, making offerings and serving the World-Honored Ones, until they became Buddhas; and all this cannot be known by language or discrimination. Whether he was born a wheel-turning king, or Indra, or the god Suyama, or a god of the Tuṣita heaven, or a god of the heaven of Good Transformation, or of the heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations, or as Great Brahma, king of the gods, in every case he was able to serve and make offerings to all the Buddhas, and to request the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma. If he was born a king of Jambudvipa, or an elder, a minister, a brahmin, or a kṣatriya, in all those clans he was able to honor and make offerings to all the Buddhas. And he could expound immeasurable Dharma-gates. Thereafter he forever abandoned the world and attained supreme enlightenment. Yet that bodhisattva could, with exquisite clothing, bedding, food, and medicine, make offerings to all Tathagatas for the whole of his life, and gain an abiding of peace and joy. All such roots of goodness brought to perfection cannot be fully bounded even by language. From his mouth there ever came the wondrous fragrance of sandalwood. That fragrance pervaded immeasurable, countless, even koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of worlds. And from every pore of his body there came the supreme fragrance of utpala flowers surpassing gods and humans. Wherever he was born, his marks and features were dignified and fair, peerless and complete. He also obtained sovereignty, the perfection of mastery, over all requisites, and every article he used was everywhere and never lacking. That is to say: jewel-incenses of every kind, flowers, banners, pennants, silken streamers, canopies, exquisite clothing, food and drink, broth and medicine, and all treasuries of hidden treasure and rare curiosities that were needed — all flowed naturally from the bodhisattva’s palms. From the pores of his body there flowed all the music of gods and humans. By these causes and conditions he was able to cause immeasurable, countless, inconceivable beings to abide in supreme, perfect enlightenment. Ananda, I have now told of the Bodhisattva Dharmakara’s original cultivation.”
At that time Ananda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, is the Bodhisattva Dharmakara, who attained bodhi, of the past? Of the future? Or is he now present in some other world?”

The Buddha told Ananda: “To the west of here, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands away, there is a world named Ultimate Bliss. There the monk Dharmakara became a Buddha, named Immeasurable Life, and he is now present, teaching the Dharma. Immeasurable bodhisattvas and assemblies of hearers revere and surround him. Ananda, the light of that Buddha illumines all Buddha-lands — immeasurable, countless, inconceivable. I shall now speak of it in brief: his light illumines the east, as many lands as the sands of the Ganges; and to the south, the west, and the north, to the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is likewise so. Except where the power of the Buddhas’ own original vows adds its majesty, all are illumined by it. The light of those Buddhas may extend one fathom, or one yojana, or even koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of yojanas, or it may illumine all Buddha-lands.

Ananda, for this reason the Buddha Immeasurable Life has other names besides, namely: Immeasurable Light, Boundless Light, Unattached Light, Unobstructed Light, Light of Majestic Sovereignty, Light of Love, Light of Joy, Light of Delight, Inconceivable Light, Unequaled Light, Immeasurable and Incommensurable Light, Light That Outshines the Sun, Light That Outshines the Moon, Light That Outshines Both Sun and Moon.

That light of his is pure and vast, causing all beings to rejoice in body and mind. And it causes all the dragons, yakṣas, asuras, and the rest in other Buddha-lands to gain gladness. Ananda, were I to open and reveal the light of that Buddha for a whole kalpa, I could not finish speaking of it.

Again, Ananda, the assembly of hearers of that Tathagata Immeasurable Life is beyond reckoning; no one can know its limit. Even if monks were as many as koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands in number, all like Mahāmaudgalyayana, with sovereign spiritual powers, who in the morning traverse a great thousand worlds and in a moment return to where they were, and they were to spend koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of years trying together to reckon the assembly of hearers at the first assembly of the Buddha Immeasurable Life — exhausting their spiritual powers, even to the end of their lives, they would not know one part in a hundred, nor one part in a thousand or a hundred thousand, nor one part in an upaniṣad either.

Ananda, it is like the great ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep: strain the eye to the utmost and its edge cannot be seen. If a man were to split the tip of a hair into fifty parts and with one of those parts take up a single drop from the great ocean — Ananda, that drop of water, compared with the great ocean, which is the greater?”
Ananda said: “Even a thousand yojanas of water would still be reckoned little, how much less could a single part of a hair’s tip be compared to it?”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Even if monks were as many as koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands in number, all like Mahāmaudgalyayana, and for a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of years they all together reckoned the assembly of hearers at the first assembly of that Tathagata Immeasurable Life, the number they could know would be like that one drop of water at a hair’s tip. The rest, beyond their measure, is like the great ocean. The assembly of bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas is likewise so, and cannot be known by reckoning. Ananda, the lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable and boundless; the number of his kalpas cannot be known. The lifespan of the hearers, the bodhisattvas, the gods, and the humans is likewise so.”
Ananda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how long has it been since that Buddha appeared in the world, that he has obtained such an immeasurable lifespan?”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Ten kalpas have passed since that Buddha took birth. Again, Ananda, that realm of Ultimate Bliss has immeasurable merit and is complete in adornment. The land is rich in harvest, and gods and humans are flourishing. Their minds and wills are harmonious and at ease, and they ever dwell in peace and security. There are no hells, no animals, and no realm of King Yama. There are fragrances of every kind, spreading their perfume everywhere. Wondrous flowers of every kind also fill the land. There are seven-treasure banners set out in rows on every side. Upon those jeweled banners hang pennants and canopies and many jeweled bells, complete in hundreds of thousands of wondrous and varied colors. Ananda, the land of that Tathagata has many jewel trees: some are of pure gold, silver, crystal, or beryl, of coral, agate, or jade; some are made of one jewel only, not mixed with others, while others are adorned with two jewels, or even up to seven. Ananda, where gold makes the tree, gold is the root and stem, and silver the leaves, flowers, and fruit. Where silver makes the tree, silver is the root and stem, and gold the leaves, flowers, and fruit. Where agate makes the tree, agate is the root and stem, and fine jade the leaves, flowers, and fruit. Where fine jade makes the tree, jade is the root and stem, and the seven treasures the leaves, flowers, and fruit. There are also gold trees with gold for the root, silver for the stem, crystal for the branches, beryl for the twigs, coral for the leaves, agate for the flowers, and fine jade for the fruit. There are also silver trees with silver for the root, gold for the stem, and the remaining branches and fruits adorned as in the gold trees. Where crystal makes the tree, crystal is the root, gold the stem, silver the branches, beryl the twigs, coral the leaves, agate the flowers, and fine jade the fruit. Beryl, pearl, agate, and the other trees are adorned with jewels in turn, all like crystal. There are also jade trees with jade for the root, gold for the stem, silver for the branches, crystal for the twigs, beryl for the leaves, coral for the flowers, and agate for the fruit. And there are immeasurable maṇi-jewel trees and other jewel-adorned trees throughout that land. Those jewel trees blaze with a radiance nothing in the world can match, and seven-treasure nets are spread over them. Those nets are soft as karpasa cotton.

Again, Ananda, the Buddha Immeasurable Life has a tree of bodhi, sixteen koṭis of yojanas tall, with branches and leaves hanging down for eight koṭis of yojanas. The trunk rises five thousand yojanas, and its girth is the same. Its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit ever bear immeasurable hundreds of thousands of wondrous colors of every kind, and precious jewels, peerlessly adorning it. That is to say: the moonlight maṇi jewel, the Śakra-abhilagna jewel, the mind-king maṇi jewel, and the sea-borne flowing maṇi jewel, whose radiance illumines everywhere, surpassing gods and humans. Upon that tree are golden locks, from which hang jeweled rosaries adorning it on every side. That is to say: rucaka jewels, musāragalva jewels, and pearls red, white, and blue, all made into rosaries. There are lion-cloud-gathering jewels and the like made into its locks, adorning its jeweled pillars. And pure gold, pearls, and various jewels and bells are made into nets. Jeweled locks adorn it, covering it over. Beryl, the ten-thousand sign, and the half-moon jewel reflect and adorn one another.

When a gentle breeze stirs them, they give forth sounds of every kind, causing all the beings of a thousand worlds, each according to the differences in what they delight in, to realize the patient acceptance of non-arising in the profound Dharma. Ananda, when the beings of those thousand worlds hear these sounds, they abide in non-retrogression from supreme bodhi. And immeasurable, countless beings obtain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.

Again, Ananda, if there are beings who see the bodhi tree, hear its sound, smell its fragrance, taste the flavor of its fruit, touch its light and shadow, or recollect the tree’s virtues, by these causes and conditions, until they reach nirvana, their five faculties are free of affliction and their minds are without distraction. All of them attain non-retrogression from supreme, perfect enlightenment.

And by seeing that bodhi tree they obtain three kinds of patient acceptance. Which three? The first is the patient acceptance that follows sound; the second is the patient acceptance of conformity; the third is the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. All this is by the majestic spirit of the original vows of the Buddha Immeasurable Life, and by his grace in the seeing; by his cultivation of meditation in past lives; because he is beyond compare; because he is without deficiency; because he cultivated well; because he received well; because he accomplished well.

blocks.text: The Assembly of Immeasurable Life Tathagata, Scroll Five, Part Two

inline.s: Again, Ananda, that realm of Ultimate Bliss has no black mountains, no ring of iron mountains, no great ring of iron mountains, no Mount Sumeru, and the like.”
Ananda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, since the heavens of the Four Great Kings and the heaven of the Thirty-Three do not exist there, on what do the mountains rest?”

The Buddha told Ananda: “What do you think? Above Mount Sumeru there are the Yama heavens, and on up to the heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations, and the heavens of the form realm as well — on what do they rest?”
Ananda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, they rest on the power of inconceivable karma.”
The Buddha said to Ananda: “Can you know inconceivable karma?”
He answered: “No.”
The Buddha told Ananda: “Can you know the roots of goodness and the power of karma of the Buddhas and of beings?”
He answered: “No, World-Honored One. In this Dharma I am truly without confusion; it is to break the net of future doubt that I have asked this question.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “That realm of Ultimate Bliss has no seas, but it has rivers. The narrowest of those rivers is fully ten yojanas wide. The shallowest of those waters is twelve yojanas deep. Such is the measure of the depth and breadth of those rivers — some twenty or thirty yojanas, even up to a hundred. Some are exceedingly deep and broad, reaching a thousand yojanas. Their waters are cool and pure, possessing the eight qualities. The deep currents ever rush, giving forth subtle and wondrous sounds, like the hundreds of thousands of celestial musics of the gods. In the Land of Bliss those sounds are heard everywhere. Wondrous flowers of every kind drift down along the current. A gentle breeze stirs softly, giving forth fragrances of every kind. Along both banks are many sandalwood trees, with long branches and dense leaves crossing and covering the rivers. They bear fruit and open flowers, whose fragrance and radiance are a delight to behold. The multitudes of beings roam and sport there, coming and going as they wish. Some wade into the rivers, bathe in the currents, and play. They are moved by waters of the heavens that accord well with what beings desire: depth and shallowness, cold and warmth, all bend to each person’s liking. Ananda, beneath the great rivers the ground is spread with golden sand, and there are celestial fragrances no one in the world can describe, scattered on the wind and giving forth their perfumes. Mingled with the flowing water is the scent of celestial mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, covering the surface over them.

Again, Ananda, the people of that land sometimes go wandering and gather together on the riverbanks. Some do not wish to hear the sound of the rushing currents: though they have obtained the celestial ear, they never hear it at all. Some wish to hear it, and at once they understand hundreds of thousands of kinds of delightful sounds. That is to say: the sound of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; the sound of stillness; the sound of non-nature; the sound of the perfections; the sound of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; the sound of spiritual powers; the sound of non-action; the sound of non-arising and non-ceasing; the sound of quiet; the sound of border quiet; the sound of utmost quiet; the sound of great compassion and great pity; the sound of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas; the sound of consecration and receiving the position — having heard such sounds of every kind.

they obtain vast delight and joy, and they accord with observation, with disenchantment, with destruction, with quiet, with border quiet, with utmost quiet, with the flavor of meaning, with Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, with the powers and fearlessnesses, with spiritual powers, with stillness, with bodhi, with the hearers, and with nirvana.

Again, Ananda, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss one does not hear the names of evil destinies, nor the names of obstruction, affliction, or covering. There are no names of hells, of Yama, or of animals. There are no names of the eight difficulties, nor names of the feeling of suffering or of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Since even the names do not exist, how much less the actual suffering. Therefore that land is named Ultimate Bliss. Ananda, I have now spoken of the causes and conditions of Ultimate Bliss in brief. Were I to speak of them at length, a kalpa would not suffice. Again, Ananda, all the beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, whether already born, now being born, or yet to be born, all obtain such wondrous bodies, with upright form and feature and sovereign spiritual powers. Complete in the power and merit of blessing, they enjoy palaces and gardens of every kind, clothing and food, incense and flowers and rosaries. Whatever they need comes as they wish, all just as they think — like the gods of the heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations.

Again, Ananda, in that Buddha-land there is subtle food. The beings there never taste or eat it. Like the gods of the sixth heaven, as they think so it comes; such food and drink is the same as having eaten it. Their complexion and strength increase, and there is no excrement. There are also immeasurable wish-fulfilling and wondrous fragrances — perfumes and powdered incense — whose scent perfumes everywhere in that Buddha-land. And scattered flowers, banners, and pennants also fill it everywhere. Those who wish to smell the fragrance smell it as they wish; those who do not wish to, never receive it at all. There are also immeasurable exquisite garments, jeweled crowns, armlets and bracelets, earrings, rosaries, flower garlands, and belts and chains, adorned with every jewel, of immeasurable radiance and hundreds of thousands of wondrous colors, all complete and naturally upon the body. There are also nets of gold and silver, of pearls and wondrous jewels, hung with many jeweled bells, adorning it on every side. Whatever palaces, towers, or pavilions the beings need, at their pleasure and desire, high or low, long or short, broad or narrow, square or round, and with all the beds and seats spread with fine clothing and adorned with every kind of jewel, appear naturally before the beings. And each person says to himself that he dwells in his own palace.

Again, Ananda, all the beings in the land of Ultimate Bliss are without marks of difference; yet in accord with the customs of other regions they are named gods and humans. Ananda, it is like a lowly caṇḍāla before a wheel-turning king: there is no comparing them at all; majesty and virtue, and the regard of others, are wholly absent. And again, as Indra before the sixth heaven, neither majesty nor the like can reach it — gardens and palaces, clothing and varied adornments, nobility and mastery, rank and spiritual powers, and transformations beyond compare. Only in the bliss of Dharma are they without difference. Ananda, you should know that the beings of that land are like the king of the heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations.

Ananda, in that realm of Ultimate Bliss, in the morning a gentle breeze stirs on every side, neither contrary nor disordered. It blows upon all the varied flowers, and the fragrance of every kind perfumes everywhere throughout the realm. When all beings are touched in body by that wind, they are peaceful, harmonious, and well attuned, like a monk who has attained the extinction-concentration. That wind moves the groves of seven-jewel trees, and the flowers drift and gather in heaps seven men’s height. The light of every color illumines the Buddha-land. It is like a man who spreads flowers on the ground and presses them even with his hand, distributing them in mixed colors in between. Those heaps of flowers are likewise so. Those flowers are subtle and wondrous, vast and soft, like karpasa cotton. When beings step on those flowers, their feet sink four fingers deep. When they lift their feet, the flowers return as before. When the morning has passed, those flowers sink of themselves into the ground. The old flowers gone, the great earth is pure and clean. New flowers rain down again and fill it once more. Thus at midday, in the afternoon, and in the first, middle, and last watches of the night, flowers drift and gather in heaps, and it is likewise so.

Ananda, there is no vast, wondrous, and rare treasure that is not born in the realm of Ultimate Bliss. Ananda, in that Buddha-land there are seven-jewel lotuses. Each lotus has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of petals. Its petals have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rare and wondrous colors of every kind, adorned with hundreds of thousands of maṇi jewels. They are covered with jeweled nets that reflect and adorn one another. Ananda, the size of those lotuses is half a yojana, or one, two, three, or four, or even hundreds of thousands of yojanas. From each one of those flowers come thirty-six koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of rays of light. From each ray of light come thirty-six koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, their bodies like gold, complete in the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty subsidiary marks, peerlessly adorned, sending forth hundreds of thousands of rays of light that illumine the worlds everywhere. Those Buddhas all appear going to the east to teach the Dharma to the multitudes, all establishing immeasurable beings in the Buddhadharma. To the south, the west, and the north, to the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is likewise so.

Again, Ananda, the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no darkness, and no firelight. Gushing springs and lakes and ponds have no place there. Nor are there names of dwelling and attachment, of households, or of groves and gardens, nor signs to mark them out, nor any kind of young child. Nor are there signs of sun and moon, of day and night. Since in every place there is no marking out, there are no names or titles either — save where the Tathagata adds his majesty.

Ananda, all the beings of that land who are yet to be born will all reach the utmost, the place of nirvana of supreme bodhi. Why is this? Because those of fixed wrong destiny and those of undetermined destiny cannot understand and establish that cause.

Ananda, in the east there are worlds like the sands of the Ganges, and in each world Buddhas like the sands of the Ganges. Those Buddhas each and all proclaim and praise the immeasurable merit and virtue of Amitabha. To the south, the west, and the north, to the four intermediate directions, above and below, the praises of the Buddhas are likewise so. Why is this? Because beings in the Buddha-lands of other regions, hearing the name of the Tathagata Immeasurable Life, and even able to arouse a single thought of pure faith, rejoicing, loving, and delighting, all who turn their roots of goodness toward rebirth in the land of Immeasurable Life are born there according to their vows and attain non-retrogression, even to supreme, perfect enlightenment — save for those who commit the five uninterrupted evils, who slander and destroy the true Dharma, and who revile the sages.

Ananda, if there are beings who, in other Buddha-lands, arouse the bodhi-mind, single-mindedly recollect the Buddha Immeasurable Life, and constantly plant many roots of goodness, and arouse the mind and turn it toward rebirth in that land, then when that person is at the end of life, the Buddha Immeasurable Life, with the assembly of monks before and behind him, appears before that person. And following that Tathagata, he is born in that land, attains non-retrogression, and shall realize supreme, perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, Ananda, if good men and good women wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and wish to see the Buddha Immeasurable Life, they should arouse the supreme bodhi-mind. They should further single-mindedly recollect the land of Ultimate Bliss, accumulate roots of goodness, and hold and turn them toward rebirth. By this they see the Buddha, are born in that land, attain non-retrogression, and reach even supreme bodhi.

Ananda, if beings of other lands arouse the bodhi-mind but do not single-mindedly recollect the Buddha Immeasurable Life, nor constantly plant many roots of goodness, but according to their own practice turn the merit of all wholesome deeds toward that Buddha, wishing to be born there, then when this person is at the end of life the Buddha Immeasurable Life sends a transformation body which, with the assembly of monks before and behind it, appears before that person. The light and marks of that transformed Buddha are no different from the true one, and receiving and guiding him, he follows that transformed Buddha and is born in that land, attaining non-retrogression and supreme bodhi.

Ananda, if there are beings who abide in the Great Vehicle and, with a pure mind, turn toward the Tathagata Immeasurable Life even for ten thoughts, recollecting the Buddha Immeasurable Life and wishing to be born in his land, and who hear the profound Dharma and at once give rise to faith and understanding, with no doubt in their minds, and even attain a single thought of pure mind, arousing a single thought to recollect the Buddha Immeasurable Life, then when that person is at the end of life, as if in a dream he sees the Buddha Immeasurable Life, and is certain to be born in that land and attain non-retrogression and supreme bodhi. Ananda, because of this benefit and meaning, the Tathagatas of immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled, boundless worlds all together praise the merit and virtue of the Buddha Immeasurable Life.

The Buddha told Ananda: in the east there are worlds like the sands of the Ganges, and in each world there are bodhisattvas like the sands of the Ganges. Wishing to behold and make offerings to the Buddha Immeasurable Life and the assemblies of sages, they come to where the Buddha is. To the south, the west, and the north, to the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is likewise so. At that time the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
The Buddha-lands of the east, in number like the sands of the Ganges.
In Buddha-lands such as these, bodhisattvas as many as those sands.
All come manifesting spiritual powers, to bow to the Buddha Immeasurable Life.
